stories.headline: After Midterm Rout, Iran War and Hegseth Take the Heat
stories.dek: Vance blames the war for GOP losses while Trump says Hegseth is staying and Democrats prepare investigations.
pole_a_bullets: The Iran campaign addressed a real threat, and Trump says it will prove worth it long-term.
Midterm losses by a sitting president's party are normal, and cost of living drove votes more than any one policy.
Hegseth is doing a good job, and swapping Pentagon chiefs mid-war during a lame duck risks disruption.
Democratic subpoenas and impeachment talk are partisan theater meant to score points, not find wrongdoing.
pole_b_bullets: Voters punished a war that raised gas prices, killed and wounded troops and drained munitions stocks.
Hegseth declared victory in April, yet fighting went on for months. That is a credibility problem.
Two years of thin oversight ends now. Congress has a duty to examine the war, the boat strikes and the general-officer firings.
Even Republicans such as Massie and Vance say the war is the problem, so this isn't only a partisan complaint.
stories.pole_a_who: Positions commonly voiced by Trump allies, Pentagon spokespeople and GOP defenders of the Iran campaign.
stories.pole_b_who: Positions commonly voiced by congressional Democrats such as Rep. Jason Crow, plus war-skeptic Republicans.
evidence_left: CBS News projects Democrats won both the House and the Senate, with at least 54 Senate seats. Alaska and Mississippi were unresolved.
Trump's approval was 38% and 89% of voters called cost of living a major factor, per CBS News.
evidence_right: Vance said "The reason we lost is the war." Trump acknowledged the war hurt Republicans but called Hegseth's work "great" (ABC News).
Rep. Thomas Massie plans to reintroduce eight articles of impeachment against Hegseth next week (The Hill).
stories.sources_line: Sourced from CBS News, ABC News, The Hill, PBS NewsHour and CBC, November 5, 2026.

stories.headline: Newsom Moves to Commute All 548 California Death Sentences
stories.dek: The governor, who is leaving office, announced the mass commutation two days after the midterms, and the state Supreme Court must approve many of the cases.
pole_a_bullets: Juries, judges and voters upheld these sentences, and one governor shouldn't erase them unilaterally.
Victims' families say it tells them the killers' lives matter more. Polly Klaas's father, Marc, called it a "knife in the back."
Waiting until after Election Day looks like avoiding voter judgment on a deeply unpopular move.
Life without parole isn't the punishment the courts imposed for the worst crimes.
pole_b_bullets: State-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California's values and diminishes everyone, Newsom argues.
Death sentences in the state fall more often on Black and Hispanic defendants and vary sharply by county.
The system is costly and slow, and executions have been on hold since the 2019 moratorium. This ends the limbo.
Prisoners will die in prison under life without parole, and the order bars them from new parole-style resentencing.
stories.pole_a_who: Positions commonly voiced by prosecutors, district attorney associations, victims' rights groups and police.
stories.pole_b_who: Positions commonly voiced by the ACLU, anti-death-penalty coalitions, faith groups and Newsom.
evidence_left: California has 548 people on death row, the most in the U.S. Newsom issued an execution moratorium in 2019.
Newsom said 382 of the cases involve multiple felony convictions and need California Supreme Court approval (NBC News).
evidence_right: Per the Marshall Project, only about 440 death-row commutations have happened nationwide since 1972, and this could cut the U.S. death-row population by nearly a third.
Newsom wrote that California voters voted to keep the death penalty on the books and that he respects that (via Yahoo/Politico reporting).
stories.sources_line: Sourced from NBC News, CalMatters, The Marshall Project, Fox News and CBC, November 5, 2026.

stories.headline: Nasdaq Enters Correction as Investors Fear Tougher AI Rules
stories.dek: A selloff in AI and chip stocks followed the Democratic midterm sweep and renewed debate over how fast to build data centers.
pole_a_bullets: The data-center buildout is the engine of recent growth, and slowing it by permit or politics would waste a lead.
Heavy rules on infrastructure hand ground to China in the AI race.
Much of the selloff reflects valuation and technical selling, so the regulatory fear is overstated.
A single federal framework beats a patchwork of state rules that raises compliance costs for builders.
pole_b_bullets: A debt-fueled buildout with unproven returns deserves scrutiny before more capital is committed.
Local opposition to data centers over power, water and cost is a democratic signal, not an obstacle to be removed.
Voters just rejected the AI industry's political influence, per CNBC. Accountability follows.
The U.S. has no comprehensive federal AI law, and basic transparency rules, as in California's SB 53, are modest.
stories.pole_a_who: Positions commonly voiced by AI and chip executives, pro-buildout investors and federal-preemption advocates.
stories.pole_b_who: Positions commonly voiced by Democratic lawmakers, state AI regulators, local data-center opponents and AI-safety advocates.
evidence_left: The Nasdaq Composite fell 5.5% to about 24,315, a correction of over 10% from its Oct. 6 record. Nvidia fell about 9% (CBS News).
The selloff erased roughly $3 trillion of S&P 500 market value (Globe and Mail/Reuters).
evidence_right: Yahoo Finance noted AI and chip stocks were already under pressure over whether infrastructure spending could earn adequate returns.
White & Case's tracker says the U.S. has no comprehensive federal AI legislation, leaving rules to states such as California and Texas.
stories.sources_line: Sourced from CBS News, Charles Schwab, Fox Business, Globe and Mail, CNBC, Yahoo Finance and White & Case, November 5, 2026.

stories.headline: October Jobs Report Looms as Fed Weighs a December Hike
stories.dek: Forecasters expect modest hiring and 4.2% unemployment, while traders put a December rate hike above 80%.
pole_a_bullets: Layoffs are scarce. Jobless claims of 189,000 are near the lowest since 1969.
Third-quarter GDP grew 3.4%, and job openings and quits both rose in September.
A "low hire, low fire" market at 4.2% unemployment is stable, not weak.
A hawkish Fed signals confidence in the economy and should anchor inflation expectations.
pole_b_bullets: September payrolls were just 29,000, and July was revised to a net loss.
Long-term unemployment is worsening, and job growth has averaged about 45,000 a month over the past year.
Hiking into weak hiring with a 10-year yield near 5% risks tipping the economy over.
Energy-driven inflation isn't something rate hikes fix, and the stock selloff shows fragility.
stories.pole_a_who: Positions commonly voiced by Wall Street strategists and economists who see labor-market resilience.
stories.pole_b_who: Positions commonly voiced by labor economists, worker advocates and rate-hike skeptics.
evidence_left: The Fed held at 3.75%-4.00% on Oct. 28 after its first hike in three years in September. Cook and Hammack dissented in favor of a hike (Schwab).
CME FedWatch odds of a December hike exceed 80% (Investopedia).
evidence_right: Economists expect 59,000 October jobs and 4.2% unemployment, after 29,000 jobs in September (CNBC).
The BLS report is due Friday, Nov. 6. Q3 GDP grew 3.4% (Kiplinger).
stories.sources_line: Sourced from CNBC, Charles Schwab, Investopedia/AOL, Morningstar, Kiplinger and Yahoo Finance, November 5, 2026.

stories.headline: Wendy's Rejects $1.4 Billion Peltz-Led Buyout, Adopts Poison Pill
stories.dek: The board says the $7.35-a-share offer undervalues its turnaround while U.S. sales keep falling.
pole_a_bullets: The board says the bid substantially undervalues the company's standalone prospects and earnings potential.
Wendy's beat Q3 expectations, and CEO Bob Wright says early progress on "Dave's Way" shows the best days are ahead.
The offer sat below where shares traded ($7.35 vs. $7.75 pre-market), so rejecting it protects holders.
The poison pill keeps a 16% holder from creeping to control without paying a fair premium.
pole_b_bullets: U.S. same-store sales fell for a seventh straight quarter, down 5.7%, so the turnaround is still unproven.
Consumer belt-tightening and franchisee distress, such as the Meritage Hospitality bankruptcy, point to sector risk.
A rights plan can entrench management, and Trian refused a standstill agreement.
If traffic doesn't recover, shareholders may regret passing up a cash exit.
stories.pole_a_who: Positions commonly voiced by Wendy's board, management and turnaround-minded investors.
stories.pole_b_who: Positions commonly voiced by activist investors, restaurant analysts and governance critics.
evidence_left: A unanimous independent committee rejected the Trian-led $1.4 billion offer of $7.35 a share, per CBS News and Bloomberg.
The board adopted a one-year shareholder rights plan after the group declined a standstill (Investing.com).
evidence_right: Trian held about 16% of Wendy's as of mid-2026, with partners Flynn Group, BlueFive Capital and Sixth Street.
Shares rose about 1.4% on the news, while U.S. same-store sales fell 5.7% in the quarter.
stories.sources_line: Sourced from CNBC, CBS News, Bloomberg, Benzinga, Law360 and Investing.com, November 5, 2026.

stories.headline: LIV Golf Winds Down After Five Years and Billions in Saudi Money
stories.dek: Lawyers told a bankruptcy court the "LIV 2.0" plan is dead, leaving stars such as DeChambeau to weigh their futures.
pole_a_bullets: LIV was always a vanity project. With no long-term U.S. TV deal, its audience and revenue never materialized.
Guaranteed payouts and no relegation stakes made it a hard league to take seriously as sport.
Roughly $5 billion invested and about $3 billion in net operating losses show the model never worked.
The PGA Tour's tradition-and-merit model was vindicated, and players who left should earn their way back.
pole_b_bullets: LIV forced the sport to pay players more and to try team formats and new presentation.
Its collapse is about Saudi funding pulling out in April, not golf fans rejecting the product.
Losing a rival employer hurts player leverage and fan choice.
The Tour's one-year bans and limited re-entry for Rahm and DeChambeau look vindictive now that the league is dead.
stories.pole_a_who: Positions commonly voiced by PGA Tour loyalists and golf traditionalists.
stories.pole_b_who: Positions commonly voiced by LIV-sympathetic players, player-leverage advocates and some analysts.
evidence_left: LIV attorneys said in New Jersey bankruptcy court on Nov. 5 that the company will not pursue LIV 2.0 and will wind down. It filed for Chapter 11 on Sept. 8.
Court filings show Saudi Arabia's PIF invested about $5 billion, and LIV had about $3 billion in net operating losses (UPI).
evidence_right: Koepka, Rahm, Reed and Garcia had already left LIV. Rahm gave up claims reportedly worth about $100 million to exit his contract.
The PGA Tour says its Returning Member Program won't be open to Rahm and DeChambeau (CBS Sports).
stories.sources_line: Sourced from CBS News, CBS Sports, UPI, Front Office Sports, Yahoo Sports and The Athletic via Mediaite, November 5, 2026.
